source.title: Restricting Trainable Lie-Algebra Growth in Equivariant Quantum Networks via Hierarchical Ancilla-Controlled Subspace Projections
source.authors: Ting Li; Zhiming Xiao; Qibiao Tang

record.tranche_reason: The paper studies trainability and training outcomes in equivariant quantum circuits. Its results do not test the classical-network behaviors named in V1–V6.
record.gate_note: The paper reports initialization-gradient comparisons and quantum-model benchmark training outcomes. These concern quantum circuits and do not measure any claim version's named behavior.
record.test_reason: The study tests quantum-circuit architecture and initialization-gradient statistics, whereas V1–V6 concern specific classical neural-network training behaviors. It neither tests nor uses those behaviors. All circuits use the same initialization distribution; the study does not compare initialization schemes as V4 requires.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate. The authors establish a structural bound on trainable Lie-algebra growth and report slower initialization-gradient decay in finite-size SU(2) simulations, alongside successful invariant learning benchmarks. They explicitly qualify that the bound does not guarantee avoidance of barren plateaus independently of the loss, observable, data, initialization and depth.
record.recipe_differences: The study proposes a hierarchical ancilla-controlled quantum-circuit architecture; it does not apply the original classical neural-network recipes in the claim versions.
record.method_sensitivity: Gradient variance and mean squared gradient norm decline as ancilla size increases from m = 1 to m = 2; hierarchical projection control retains larger values than global control at each tested m.

fits_no_version.finding: Across 4–12 data qubits, the hierarchical SU(2) circuit has slower initialization-gradient variance decay and larger mean squared gradient norms than the generic and conventional equivariant baselines. At eight qubits its gradient-norm distribution also has a higher central range.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Under the tested uniform initialization and ideal finite-size simulation, hierarchical SU(2) control preserves larger initialization-gradient statistics than the compared quantum circuits.

fits_no_version.finding: Increasing ancilla size from one to two qubits lowers both gradient measures in both architectures; hierarchical projection control retains larger values than global control at each tested size.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In the tested quantum circuits, hierarchical control improves initialization-gradient statistics relative to global control, while adding ancilla qubits alone does not.

fits_no_version.finding: The proposed model reaches approximately 0.97 sphere–torus test accuracy, outperforms matched HEA on sparse ModelNet-5, and reaches normalized Heisenberg energy training MSE near 0.04.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The tested hierarchical SU(2) architecture retains capacity for the reported invariant learning tasks and improves early optimization and accuracy over HEA on sparse ModelNet-5.

record.code_released: not stated; code and simulation results are available from the corresponding author upon reasonable request.
record.problems: The trainability comparisons are finite-size exact state-vector simulations with no numerical values transcribed from Figures 4 and 5. Hardware noise and finite-shot sampling are absent. The authors note that gradient behavior depends on loss, data distribution, initialization, observable, and depth; they state the structural bound is not a loss-independent guarantee against barren plateaus.

untested.parts: All parts: classical convolutional networks, CIFAR training classification error, label corruption, model size, training duration and regularization.
All parts: two-layer ReLU teacher–student optimization, spurious local minima and extra student neurons.
All parts: depth-related training degradation in plain classical networks, identity shortcuts, special tanh initialization and Fixup.
All parts: activation-matched initialization, signal propagation across classical-network depth, learning speed, orthogonal versus Gaussian weights and trainable convolutional depth.
All parts: learning-rate stability thresholds, transient loss growth and recovery, curvature reduction, edge-of-stability dynamics and divergence.
All parts: batch normalization's effect on training speed and learning-rate tolerance, and comparable normalization-free training with Fixup.

record.verdict_notes: All rows remain linked to none. Their cannot_determine states indicate that their measures cannot establish V1–V6, rather than uncertainty about the qualitative quantum-circuit findings. No omitted result in the supplied text bears on these versions.

versions.untested_parts: Classical convolutional networks, CIFAR-10/CIFAR-100 training classification error, random or corrupted labels, model size and training duration.
Two-layer ReLU teacher-student problems, spurious minima, and student width relative to teacher width.
Plain versus residual classical networks, depth-dependent training error, batch normalization, special initialization, and normalization-free residual training.
Activation-matched initialization, signal and gradient propagation across classical network depth, orthogonal versus Gaussian initialization, and 10,000-layer convolutional training.
Learning-rate stability thresholds, loss recovery or divergence, curvature and sharpness in classical networks.
Batch normalization effects on classical network training speed and learning-rate tolerance, and Fixup residual training.

rows.subject: hierarchical ancilla-controlled architecture instantiated with SU (2) sector projectors

rows.subject: hierarchical ancilla-controlled architecture instantiated with SU (2) sector projectors
rows.size_stated: N = 4 data qubits; m = 1 shared ancilla qubit; circuit depth 5
rows.operation_detail: Trained on sampled sphere and torus point-cloud binary classification with Adam and mean squared error.
rows.value: quickly exceeds 0.9 in the early training stage and stabilizes around 0.97
rows.note: Quantum-circuit benchmark; this does not measure the classification-error behavior in the claim versions.
rows.check: Sphere–torus test accuracy in a quantum model does not measure CIFAR training classification error or any other version. The numerical paraphrase matches the text.

rows.subject: proposed architecture
rows.size_stated: m = 5; quantum circuit contains 380 parameters and classical head contains 181, for 561 parameters in total
rows.operation_detail: Trained on ModelNet-5 sparse point-cloud classification; the quantum circuit uses 4 points per object.
rows.note: Authors also report the proposed architecture decreases loss faster during early training.
rows.check: This is the proposed quantum–classical method's validation performance against HEA, outside V1–V6. Faster early loss reduction is an architecture comparison, not an initialization or batch-normalization experiment.

rows.subject: proposed architecture
rows.size_stated: m = 5; quantum circuit contains 380 parameters and classical head contains 181, for 561 parameters in total
rows.operation_detail: Evaluated test accuracy on ModelNet-5 sparse point-cloud classification.
rows.note: Results are compared with a hardware-efficient ansatz using matched numbers of data and ancilla qubits and comparable quantum and classical parameter counts.
rows.check: This is the proposed method's test-accuracy comparison with HEA, not evidence on any claim version. The reported 75.6 ± 0.8% versus 50.5 ± 1.2% matches the text.

rows.subject: hierarchical ancilla-controlled architecture instantiated with SU (2) sector projectors
rows.size_stated: N = 4 data qubits; m = 1 shared ancilla qubit; circuit depth 4
rows.operation_detail: Trained to regress geometry-dependent Heisenberg ground-state energy using Adam and normalized labels.

conditions.value: 600 samples; 480 for training and 120 for testing

rows.note: The paper also reports test MSE approximately 4 × 10−2.
rows.check: Quantum energy-regression training MSE does not measure any version. MSE near 0.04 cannot be classified as partial near-zero classification error under V1.
